title: Domain-Specific Accelerators
summary: Where the specialization spectrum goes past the GPU, and why a fixed-function chip can beat a programmable one at the one job it's built for.

slides.markdown:
Hardware sits on a spectrum from fully general to fully fixed: a **general-purpose CPU** runs any program but wastes silicon on flexibility it doesn't always need; a **programmable GPU** narrows that flexibility to data-parallel workloads and gets more throughput per watt in exchange; a **fixed-function ASIC** (application-specific integrated circuit) gives up programmability almost entirely for one job, done as efficiently as physics allows.

Every step along this spectrum trades **generality for efficiency**. Nothing about the trend is new — it's the same trade a GPU already makes relative to a CPU, just pushed one step further.

A general-purpose core spends real silicon and power on capabilities most workloads never use: branch prediction for code paths that don't exist, instruction decoders for opcodes never issued, cache hierarchies sized for arbitrary access patterns. A chip built for exactly one operation skips all of that.

The result is often a **10–100x** improvement in performance-per-watt for that one operation — because every transistor on the die is doing useful work for the specific task, instead of standing ready for tasks that will never arrive on this chip.

A **TPU** (Tensor Processing Unit) is Google's accelerator built specifically for the matrix multiplications that dominate neural network training and inference. Its core is a **systolic array**: a grid of simple multiply-accumulate units where data flows through in a fixed rhythm, each cell passing partial results to its neighbor every cycle.

This works because matrix multiply has an extremely regular, predictable dataflow — unlike a GPU, which still fetches instructions and manages threads generically, a systolic array hardwires the *pattern itself* into silicon, eliminating almost all instruction-level overhead for that one computation.

Plotting the spectrum as two opposing axes makes the trade-off explicit: as flexibility drops, efficiency for the target task rises.

![A spectrum from CPU to GPU to ASIC, with flexibility decreasing and efficiency for the target task increasing left to right](assets/specialization-spectrum.svg)

No point on this line is universally "correct" — a chip that's efficient at one thing is, by construction, less useful for everything else. Choosing where to sit on this spectrum is a bet on how narrow and how stable the target workload is.

slides.markdown:
For machine learning workloads specifically, the choice between GPU and TPU/ASIC comes down to programmability versus peak efficiency.

| | GPU | TPU / ML ASIC |
|---|---|---|
| Programmability | General — any kernel, any framework | Narrow — tuned for matrix-multiply-heavy ops |
| Efficiency at target op | Good | Better — often higher perf/watt |
| Flexibility to pivot | Easy — new model architectures, custom ops | Harder — non-matmul-heavy ops may not map well |

Teams iterating on novel model architectures often stay on GPUs for flexibility; teams running a stable, matmul-dominated workload at massive scale (e.g., serving one well-established model) gain the most from moving to a TPU/ASIC.

It's tempting to think of an ASIC like a TPU as simply "a faster GPU," but that undersells the trade it actually made. A GPU is still programmable — it can run an enormous range of kernels, including ones that look nothing like matrix multiply.

An ASIC typically supports a **much narrower set of operations**, often just the handful its designers targeted. Feed it a workload outside that set — an operation the systolic array wasn't built to express — and it may run poorly, need to fall back to a slower general path, or simply not be expressible on the chip at all. Specialization is exactly what makes it fast, and exactly what makes it narrow.
